draft.title: Nonconformity
card: Nonconformity is going against the norms and expectations of a group or society. A norm is an unwritten rule about how people are expected to behave.
Personal choice
a person acts differently because of their own values or tastes, such as a student who dresses unlike their friends.
Protest
a person or group breaks a norm on purpose to show disagreement and call for change, such as a sit-in against a rule they think is unfair.
New group
people who reject the norms around them may join others who think alike. Together they can form a new group with its own norms.
draft.remember: Nonconformity means going against norms, for personal, protest or group-forming reasons.

opts: Sam wears his hair in a style no one else at school has
Sam joins the school choir because all his friends did
Sam follows the dress code at every school event
Sam copies his team's habits to fit in with them
a.why: Sam goes against what is usual at his school, so this is nonconformity. Joining the choir with friends is the opposite, as it follows what the group does.
a.clue: Which one goes against what the group usually does?

b.q: Residents of a Perth suburb all keep tidy front lawns. Nina replaces hers with a wild native garden and puts up a sign saying lawns waste water. Why is her action a protest as well as nonconformity?
opts: She breaks the norm on purpose to argue for change
She dislikes lawns and has a different taste in plants
She wants to be accepted by her neighbours
She is following the rules of her local council
b.why: Nina breaks the norm and uses the sign to argue for change, which makes it a protest. A different taste alone would be a personal choice, and the sign shows she wants more than that.
b.clue: Look at what the sign adds to her choice.

a.best: Sam wears his hair in a style no one else at school has

b.best: She breaks the norm on purpose to argue for change

problems.detail: The card defines a norm as 'an unwritten rule'. Norms include written, formal rules too, such as school dress codes and laws, and point 3 refers to formal sanctions such as laws. Question a itself uses a dress code, which is written, as its example of following a norm. Better: 'A norm is an expected way of behaving in a group, whether written or unwritten.'

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer, and the explanations match the card. The card's definition of a norm as only 'unwritten' is too narrow and clashes with the dress-code example in question a.
